stories.title: Four patterns for staying in control of an agent
stories.blurb: A former Xerox-lineage UX researcher runs today’s agentic interfaces back through Lucy Suchman’s 1980s photocopier study and lands on four concrete patterns: calibrated uncertainty with visible provenance, mid-run steering that does not reset the agent’s progress, shared surfaces where several stakeholders can interrogate the reasoning, and progressive disclosure of the machine’s logic. The argument underneath is that fluent prose hides the sensory gap rather than closing it.

stories.title: Open an AI product with an answer, not a question
stories.blurb: Wroblewski replaced the empty prompt on his site’s Ask feature with a daily compiled answer about what he has been writing and reading. His usability testing had already shown that merely reading suggested questions helped people understand what the product could do; putting an answer above them attacks capability awareness head on.

stories.title: The repair move that works, and the one everyone reaches for
stories.blurb: A Stanford team analysed 249,834 real conversations and found friction in 49.7 percent of them. Challenging the model’s reasoning was productive 81.5 percent of the time, while rephrasing the same request in new words failed 19.8 percent. The uncomfortable part: critique drops off in the highest-stakes tasks, precisely where oversight matters most.

stories.title: Guinness modernises by moving its harp, not redrawing it
stories.blurb: AMV BBDO’s LoVely campaign swaps the “v” in the word for the harp that has sat on the bottle for over 160 years. The mark was not distorted to fit, and that is the point: the silhouette already read as a “v”, which makes this an argument for finding what is hiding in a heritage asset instead of drawing a new one.

sources.headline: This clever design trick by Guinness means it can modernise without needing a new logo

stories.title: Solving the sponsor lockup one level below the logo
stories.blurb: For British Cycling’s national series with headline partner Lloyds, Form cut custom letterforms from Anton that take their curves from both the British Cycling Vic and the Lloyds horse. Creative director Alex Andlaw’s account is that carrying both brands in the typography meant the equal-weight lockup argument never started.

sources.headline: How Form solved the classic two-logo lockup problem for British Cycling and its sponsor, Lloyds

stories.title: An archive turned into working material
stories.blurb: Baby Teeth’s rebrand of the 272-year-old Royal Society of Arts treats the archive as raw material rather than decoration, with historic collisions, vertically sliced portraits and offset crops built to interrupt continuity across the journal and RSA House. The monogram comes from the six-lobed rosette in the building’s oculus facade, with a dropped, angled A.

stories.title: A categorical palette as an optimisation problem
stories.blurb: Ström-Awn’s second version of his colour algorithm ships as an npm package with a GUI and adds evaluators for just-noticeable difference, WCAG AA contrast against a chosen background, and how easily a colour can be named. The premise holds from the first version: there are no right colours, only the least wrong ones for a stated cost function.

stories.title: OpenAI cannot rule out that user work improved its model
stories.blurb: Mathematician Tristan Buckmaster says OpenAI leaned on him after learning of his Navier-Stokes progress, including a suggestion to drop his Anthropic-employed coauthor. OpenAI denies accessing specific user data but concedes it “cannot rule out that de-identified data derived from their usage of our products helped improve our models”. That sentence is the part worth reading if you put unpublished work into a lab’s tools.

stories.title: Koto starts buying studios
stories.blurb: Backed by 2025 investment from Westbridge, Koto has acquired Stereo Creative and taken the group from 170 to 230 people across eight hubs, with further founder-led acquisitions planned. The stated driver is client demand for brand, digital, campaign and content work under one roof.

stories.title: Apple signs the photo in the sensor
stories.blurb: Reference Image on the iPhone 18 Pro signs sensor data at capture and develops it through Private Cloud Compute into a version that cannot be altered, so later edits can be compared against it. There is an API for third-party apps across iOS, iPadOS and macOS. It does not ship in the EU at launch.

stories.title: Suno rebuilds on licensed data and retires everything older
stories.blurb: Suno v6 was developed with Warner Music Group, BMG and Believe after a run of copyright suits, and the company says it does not use the data behind earlier versions. All previous models are being retired. A planned remix programme would let rights holders opt in for a share of revenue.
